item.title: Boundedness, Supremum, and Infimum
item.author: y.zhao.phys@gmail.com (Yijia Zhao)
item.dc:creator: Yijia Zhao
item.description: A practical guide to proving boundedness and working with suprema and infima, with an emphasis on quantifiers and choosing suitable elements.
item.content:encoded:
1. Foundations

Let us begin with a brief review of the definitions.

Definition 1 — Boundedness

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R}. We say that AA is bounded above if there exists M∈RM \in \mathbb{R} such that a≤Ma \leq M for every a∈Aa \in A. Any such MM is called an upper bound of AA.

Similarly, AA is bounded below if there exists m∈Rm \in \mathbb{R} such that m≤am \leq a for every a∈Aa \in A. Any such mm is called a lower bound of AA.

The set AA is bounded if it is both bounded above and bounded below. Thus,

A is bounded  ⟺  (A is bounded above)∧(A is bounded below). A \text{ is bounded} \iff \bigl(A \text{ is bounded above}\bigr) \land \bigl(A \text{ is bounded below}\bigr).

In particular, the empty set is bounded: every real number is both an upper bound and a lower bound of ∅\varnothing, since there are no elements that could violate either condition.

Definition 2 — Supremum and infimum

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R}. A real number ss is the supremum (or least upper bound) of AA, written s=sup⁡As = \sup A, if:

  1. a≤sa \leq s for every a∈Aa \in A;
  2. s≤Ms \leq M for every upper bound M∈RM \in \mathbb{R} of AA.

Similarly, a real number tt is the infimum (or greatest lower bound) of AA, written t=inf⁡At = \inf A, if:

  1. t≤at \leq a for every a∈Aa \in A;
  2. m≤tm \leq t for every lower bound m∈Rm \in \mathbb{R} of AA.

To include unbounded sets and the empty set, we also allow values in the extended real line R‾=R∪{−∞,+∞}\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}, ordered by −∞<x<+∞-\infty \lt x \lt +\infty for every x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}. We adopt the conventions

sup⁡A=+∞if A is not bounded above,inf⁡A=−∞if A is not bounded below,sup⁡∅=−∞,inf⁡∅=+∞.\begin{aligned} \sup A &= +\infty &&\text{if } A \text{ is not bounded above}, \\ \inf A &= -\infty &&\text{if } A \text{ is not bounded below}, \\ \sup \varnothing &= -\infty, \qquad &\inf \varnothing &= +\infty. \end{aligned}

These conventions agree with taking the least upper bound and greatest lower bound in R‾\overline{\mathbb{R}}. The empty set has no supremum or infimum in R\mathbb{R} itself.

Axiom 3 — Completeness of the real numbers

Every nonempty subset of R\mathbb{R} that is bounded above has a supremum in R\mathbb{R}.

Every nonempty subset of R\mathbb{R} that is bounded below has an infimum in R\mathbb{R}.

The second statement follows from the first by applying it to −A={−a:a∈A}-A = \{-a : a \in A\} and using inf⁡A=−sup⁡(−A)\inf A = -\sup(-A). We state both together here for ease of reference.

Theorem 4 — Archimedean property

For every x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}, there exists a positive integer nn such that x<nx \lt n. In other words, the positive integers are not bounded above in R\mathbb{R}.

Lemma 5 — Integer bracketing

For every x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}, there exists an integer n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z} such that

n−1≤x<n. n - 1 \leq x \lt n.

We will not go into further proofs or explanations here; for details, see the notes.

2. Proof Strategies

We now examine in detail how to prove the various properties introduced above.

2.1. Boundedness

To prove boundedness, we find fixed real bounds that work for every element of the set.

Remark 6

Let A⊆RA\subseteq\mathbb{R}. Then

A is bounded above  ⟺  ∃M∈R  ∀a∈A,a≤M,A is bounded below  ⟺  ∃m∈R  ∀a∈A,m≤a,A is bounded  ⟺  ∃m,M∈R  ∀a∈A,m≤a≤M.\begin{aligned} A\text{ is bounded above} &\iff \exists M\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall a\in A,\quad a\leq M, \\ A\text{ is bounded below} &\iff \exists m\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall a\in A,\quad m\leq a, \\ A\text{ is bounded} &\iff \exists m,M\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall a\in A,\quad m\leq a\leq M. \end{aligned}

The bounds may depend on the set and its fixed parameters, but must not depend on the individual element aa. We choose the bounds first and then verify the inequalities for arbitrary a∈Aa\in A; there is no need to find the best possible bounds.

2.2. Unboundedness

First, negating the definitions of boundedness above and below gives the following characterizations.

Remark 7

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R}. Then

A is unbounded above  ⟺  ¬(∃M∈R  ∀a∈A,  a≤M)  ⟺  ∀M∈R  ∃a∈A,  a>M,A is unbounded below  ⟺  ¬(∃m∈R  ∀a∈A,  m≤a)  ⟺  ∀m∈R  ∃a∈A,  a<m.\begin{aligned} A \text{ is unbounded above} &\iff \neg\bigl(\exists M \in \mathbb{R}\; \forall a \in A,\; a \leq M\bigr) \\ &\iff \forall M \in \mathbb{R}\; \exists a \in A,\; a > M, \\ A \text{ is unbounded below} &\iff \neg\bigl(\exists m \in \mathbb{R}\; \forall a \in A,\; m \leq a\bigr) \\ &\iff \forall m \in \mathbb{R}\; \exists a \in A,\; a \lt m. \end{aligned}

In other words, to prove that AA is unbounded above, we start with an arbitrary proposed upper bound M∈RM \in \mathbb{R} and find an element a∈Aa \in A with a>Ma > M. Our choice of aa may depend on MM: when giving an explicit construction, we express aa in terms of MM and verify both that a∈Aa \in A and that a>Ma > M.

Likewise, to prove that AA is unbounded below, we start with an arbitrary m∈Rm \in \mathbb{R} and choose a∈Aa \in A, depending on mm, such that a<ma \lt m. The order of the quantifiers matters: the proposed bound is given first, and we then choose an element that exceeds it or falls below it.

Let us illustrate this with a simple example.

Example 8 — The real line is unbounded

The set A={x∣x∈R}=RA = \{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R}\} = \mathbb{R} is unbounded both above and below.

Proof.

Given any M∈RM \in \mathbb{R}, choose a=M+1a = M + 1. Then a∈Aa \in A and a>Ma > M, so AA is unbounded above.

Similarly, given any m∈Rm \in \mathbb{R}, choose a=m−1a = m - 1. Then a∈Aa \in A and a<ma \lt m, so AA is unbounded below. Hence AA is unbounded.

□

2.3. Identifying a Supremum or Infimum

To prove that a real number ss is the supremum of AA, we must show that it is an upper bound and that it is the least upper bound. For the second part, we show that every number strictly smaller than ss, written as s−εs - \varepsilon with ε>0\varepsilon > 0, fails to be an upper bound.

Remark 9

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R} and s,t∈Rs,t \in \mathbb{R}. Then s=sup⁡As = \sup A if and only if both of the following hold:

  1. ss is an upper bound: ∀a∈A,a≤s. \forall a \in A,\quad a \leq s.
  2. For every ε>0\varepsilon > 0, s−εs - \varepsilon is not an upper bound: ∀ε>0  ∃a∈A,s−ε<a. \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists a \in A,\quad s - \varepsilon \lt a.

Similarly, t=inf⁡At = \inf A if and only if both of the following hold:

  1. tt is a lower bound: ∀a∈A,t≤a. \forall a \in A,\quad t \leq a.
  2. For every ε>0\varepsilon > 0, t+εt + \varepsilon is not a lower bound: ∀ε>0  ∃a∈A,a<t+ε. \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists a \in A,\quad a \lt t + \varepsilon.

The two parts require different approaches. To establish the bound, take an arbitrary a∈Aa \in A and prove the required inequality. To establish that the bound is the least or greatest one, take an arbitrary ε>0\varepsilon > 0 and find a suitable a∈Aa \in A. Here the candidate ss or tt is fixed, and our choice of aa may depend on ε\varepsilon: in an explicit construction, we express aa in terms of ε\varepsilon (and the fixed candidate ss or tt).

For a supremum, the chosen element must satisfy s−ε<a≤ss - \varepsilon \lt a \leq s; for an infimum, it must satisfy t≤a<t+εt \leq a \lt t + \varepsilon. In each case, we must verify that the chosen element belongs to AA. The element need not equal the supremum or infimum; it only needs to lie within the prescribed distance on the appropriate side.

Example 10 — A supremum that is not attained

Let

A={1−1x  |  x∈R+}, A = \left\{1 - \frac{1}{x} \;\middle|\; x \in \mathbb{R}_{+}\right\},

where R+=(0,∞)\mathbb{R}_{+} = (0,\infty). Then sup⁡A=1\sup A = 1.

Proof.

First, for every x>0x > 0, we have 1/x>01/x > 0, so 1−1/x<11 - 1/x \lt 1. Thus every a∈Aa \in A satisfies a≤1a \leq 1, and 11 is an upper bound of AA.

Next, let ε>0\varepsilon > 0 be arbitrary. To show that 1−ε1 - \varepsilon is not an upper bound, we need an x>0x > 0 such that

1−1x>1−ε, 1 - \frac{1}{x} > 1 - \varepsilon,

which is equivalent to x>1/εx > 1/\varepsilon. Choose x=2/ε>0x = 2/\varepsilon > 0. Then a=1−1/xa = 1 - 1/x belongs to AA and

a=1−ε2>1−ε. a = 1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} > 1 - \varepsilon.

Hence 1−ε1 - \varepsilon is not an upper bound for any ε>0\varepsilon > 0. Therefore sup⁡A=1\sup A = 1.

□

In Section 3, we will discuss more systematically how to solve inequalities of this kind and choose suitable elements of the set.

There is also a simpler way to identify a supremum when the proposed upper bound belongs to the set itself.

Theorem 11 — Attained bounds are suprema and infima

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R} and s,t∈Rs,t \in \mathbb{R}. If ss is an upper bound of AA and s∈As \in A, then sup⁡A=s\sup A = s.

Similarly, if tt is a lower bound of AA and t∈At \in A, then inf⁡A=t\inf A = t.

The converse does not hold: s=sup⁡As = \sup A does not imply that s∈As \in A. In the preceding example, sup⁡A=1\sup A = 1, but 1∉A1 \notin A, since 1−1/x<11 - 1/x \lt 1 for every x>0x > 0.

2.4. Ruling Out a Candidate Supremum or Infimum

Taking the contrapositives of the necessary conditions in Section 2.3 gives two ways to rule out a proposed supremum or infimum. It is enough for either condition to fail.

Remark 12

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R} and let s,t∈Rs,t \in \mathbb{R} be arbitrary. Then ss is not the supremum of AA if either of the following holds:

  1. There exists ε>0\varepsilon > 0 such that s+ε∈As + \varepsilon \in A, so ss is not an upper bound.
  2. There exists ε>0\varepsilon > 0 such that s−εs - \varepsilon is an upper bound of AA, so ss cannot be the least upper bound.

In logical notation,

[(∃ε>0,  s+ε∈A)∨(∃ε>0  ∀a∈A,  a≤s−ε)]  ⟺  s≠sup⁡A.\begin{aligned} \Bigl[\bigl(\exists \varepsilon > 0,\; s + \varepsilon \in A\bigr) \lor \bigl(\exists \varepsilon > 0\; \forall a \in A,\; a \leq s - \varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr] \\ \iff s \neq \sup A. \end{aligned}

Similarly, tt is not the infimum of AA if either of the following holds:

  1. There exists ε>0\varepsilon > 0 such that t−ε∈At - \varepsilon \in A, so tt is not a lower bound.
  2. There exists ε>0\varepsilon > 0 such that t+εt + \varepsilon is a lower bound of AA, so tt cannot be the greatest lower bound.

In logical notation,

[(∃ε>0,  t−ε∈A)∨(∃ε>0  ∀a∈A,  t+ε≤a)]  ⟺  t≠inf⁡A.\begin{aligned} \Bigl[\bigl(\exists \varepsilon > 0,\; t - \varepsilon \in A\bigr) \lor \bigl(\exists \varepsilon > 0\; \forall a \in A,\; t + \varepsilon \leq a\bigr)\Bigr] \\ \iff t \neq \inf A. \end{aligned}

The dependence has now changed. In Section 2.3, we were given an arbitrary ε>0\varepsilon > 0 and had to choose an element aa in terms of it. Here the candidate ss or tt is fixed, and we only need to find one suitable ε>0\varepsilon > 0, chosen in terms of that candidate, to rule it out. In the second case, this single choice must work for every a∈Aa \in A, since we must show that the shifted candidate is still a bound.

Example 13 — Constructing a cube root using completeness

Let

A={x∈R∣x3<2}. A = \{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid x^3 \lt 2\}.

Then s=sup⁡As = \sup A exists and satisfies s3=2s^3 = 2.

Proof.

Since 1∈A1 \in A and 22 is an upper bound of AA, completeness gives s=sup⁡A∈Rs = \sup A \in \mathbb{R}. Moreover, 1≤s≤21 \leq s \leq 2, so s>0s > 0.

Suppose first that s3>2s^3 > 2. Choose

ε1=min⁡{s2,s3−26s2}. \varepsilon_1 = \min\left\{\frac{s}{2},\frac{s^3 - 2}{6s^2}\right\}.

Then 0<ε1≤s/2<s0 \lt \varepsilon_1 \leq s/2 \lt s, and

(s−ε1)3=s3−3s2ε1+ε12(3s−ε1)≥s3−3s2ε1≥s3−s3−22=s3+22>2.\begin{aligned} (s - \varepsilon_1)^3 &= s^3 - 3s^2\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_1^2(3s - \varepsilon_1) \\ &\geq s^3 - 3s^2\varepsilon_1 \\ &\geq s^3 - \frac{s^3 - 2}{2} \\ &= \frac{s^3 + 2}{2} > 2. \end{aligned}

For every a∈Aa \in A, we therefore have a3<2<(s−ε1)3a^3 \lt 2 \lt (s - \varepsilon_1)^3. Since cubing is strictly increasing on R\mathbb{R}, it follows that a<s−ε1a \lt s - \varepsilon_1. Thus s−ε1s - \varepsilon_1 is an upper bound of AA, contradicting the fact that ss is its least upper bound.

Suppose instead that s3<2s^3 \lt 2. Choose

ε2=min⁡{s2,2−s314s2}. \varepsilon_2 = \min\left\{\frac{s}{2},\frac{2 - s^3}{14s^2}\right\}.

Again, 0<ε2≤s/2<s0 \lt \varepsilon_2 \leq s/2 \lt s. Using ε2<s\varepsilon_2 \lt s, we obtain

(s+ε2)3=s3+3s2ε2+3sε22+ε23≤s3+7s2ε2≤s3+2−s32=s3+22<2.\begin{aligned} (s + \varepsilon_2)^3 &= s^3 + 3s^2\varepsilon_2 + 3s\varepsilon_2^2 + \varepsilon_2^3 \\ &\leq s^3 + 7s^2\varepsilon_2 \\ &\leq s^3 + \frac{2 - s^3}{2} \\ &= \frac{s^3 + 2}{2} \lt 2. \end{aligned}

Hence s+ε2∈As + \varepsilon_2 \in A. But s+ε2>ss + \varepsilon_2 > s, contradicting the fact that ss is an upper bound of AA.

Both alternatives are impossible, so s3=2s^3 = 2.

□

For now, we have simply stated suitable choices of ε1\varepsilon_1 and ε2\varepsilon_2 and checked that they work. In Section 3, we will explain how to obtain these choices systematically.

2.5. Using Known Suprema and Infima

Corollary 14 — Approximating suprema and infima by elements of the set

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R} and s,t∈Rs,t \in \mathbb{R}.

If s=sup⁡As = \sup A, then for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0 there exists x∈Ax \in A such that

s−ε<x≤s. s - \varepsilon \lt x \leq s.

Similarly, if t=inf⁡At = \inf A, then for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0 there exists x∈Ax \in A such that

t≤x<t+ε. t \leq x \lt t + \varepsilon.

In logical notation,

s=sup⁡A  ⟹  ∀ε>0  ∃x∈A,s−ε<x≤s,t=inf⁡A  ⟹  ∀ε>0  ∃x∈A,t≤x<t+ε.\begin{aligned} s = \sup A &\implies \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists x \in A,\quad s - \varepsilon \lt x \leq s, \\ t = \inf A &\implies \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists x \in A,\quad t \leq x \lt t + \varepsilon. \end{aligned}

Once we know that s=sup⁡As = \sup A or t=inf⁡At = \inf A, we can use the corresponding approximation property as an available hypothesis in another proof. We choose a positive tolerance suited to the problem, and the corollary supplies an element of AA within that tolerance of the known supremum or infimum.

Example 15 — The supremum of a reciprocal set

Let ∅≠A⊆R+\varnothing \neq A \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{+} and define

B={1x  |  x∈A}. B = \left\{\frac{1}{x} \;\middle|\; x \in A\right\}.

If t=inf⁡At = \inf A and t≠0t \neq 0, then sup⁡B=1/t\sup B = 1/t.

Proof.

Since A⊆(0,∞)A \subseteq (0,\infty), we have t≥0t \geq 0. Together with t≠0t \neq 0, this gives t>0t > 0.

First, every a∈Aa \in A satisfies a≥t>0a \geq t > 0, so 1/a≤1/t1/a \leq 1/t. Thus 1/t1/t is an upper bound of BB.

Next, let ε>0\varepsilon > 0 be arbitrary. Since t2ε>0t^2\varepsilon > 0 and t=inf⁡At = \inf A, we can apply the corollary with tolerance t2εt^2\varepsilon to obtain an a∈Aa \in A such that

t≤a<t+t2ε. t \leq a \lt t + t^2\varepsilon.

Using a≥t>0a \geq t > 0 and a−t<t2εa - t \lt t^2\varepsilon, we obtain

0≤1t−1a=a−tta≤a−tt2<t2εt2=ε. 0 \leq \frac{1}{t} - \frac{1}{a} = \frac{a-t}{ta} \leq \frac{a-t}{t^2} \lt \frac{t^2\varepsilon}{t^2} = \varepsilon.

Therefore 1/t−ε<1/a≤1/t1/t - \varepsilon \lt 1/a \leq 1/t, with 1/a∈B1/a \in B. Hence 1/t−ε1/t - \varepsilon is not an upper bound of BB. Since this holds for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0, we conclude that sup⁡B=1/t\sup B = 1/t.

□

2.6. Summary

The following table summarizes the logical goals and the order in which we choose the quantities involved. In the last two rows, the supremum or infimum is already known, so the displayed statement is available for use in a proof.

Bounded below ∃m∈R  ∀a∈A,  m≤a\exists m\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall a\in A,\;m\leq a Choose a fixed mm independent of aa, then verify the inequality for every a∈Aa\in A.

In the second alternative, the same ε\varepsilon must work for every aa.

In the second alternative, the same ε\varepsilon must work for every aa.

Using a known infimum t=inf⁡A  ⟹  ∀ε>0  ∃x∈A,  t≤x<t+εt=\inf A \implies \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists x \in A,\; t \leq x \lt t+\varepsilon Choose a positive tolerance ε\varepsilon; the corollary supplies xx depending on it.

3. Finding Suitable Choices

We now systematically collect some useful techniques for solving the inequalities that arise in these proofs.

3.1. Bounding Expressions

Our goal is to find a choice that satisfies the required inequality, rather than to determine every possible solution. We can therefore replace the original inequality with a stronger, simpler condition: any solution of that condition will also solve the original problem. This is why estimates are useful even when they are not sharp.

To prove M>xM > x, it is enough to find an intermediate quantity DD such that

M≥D>x. M \geq D > x.

Here we replace MM by a smaller or equal quantity DD and prove that even DD is greater than xx. Thus, to show that an expression is sufficiently large, we can work with a lower bound for it.

Similarly, to prove m<xm \lt x, it is enough to find an intermediate quantity dd such that

m≤d<x. m \leq d \lt x.

Here we replace mm by a larger or equal quantity dd and prove that even dd is less than xx. Thus, to show that an expression is sufficiently small, we can work with an upper bound for it.

A useful way to remember the direction is: to prove it is large, make it smaller first; to prove it is small, make it larger first. The estimate makes the task stronger, so completing it guarantees the original inequality. Keep the strict inequality at the final comparison with xx; the intermediate estimate itself may be non-strict.

Let us return to the cube-root example and work backwards from the desired inequality. Suppose that s3>2s^3 > 2. We want to choose ε>0\varepsilon > 0 so that

(s−ε)3>2. (s-\varepsilon)^3 > 2.

Expanding and rearranging gives

(s−ε)3>2  ⟺  s3−3s2ε+3sε2−ε3>2  ⟺  3s2ε−3sε2+ε3<s3−2.\begin{aligned} (s-\varepsilon)^3 > 2 &\iff s^3-3s^2\varepsilon+3s\varepsilon^2-\varepsilon^3 > 2 \\ &\iff 3s^2\varepsilon-3s\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^3 \lt s^3-2. \end{aligned}

The right-hand side is a fixed positive gap. Our task is to make the expression on the left smaller than that gap. Following the principle above, we should bound the left-hand side from above: find a simpler expression U(ε)U(\varepsilon) such that

3s2ε−3sε2+ε3≤U(ε)<s3−2. 3s^2\varepsilon-3s\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^3 \leq U(\varepsilon) \lt s^3-2.

If even this larger expression lies below the gap, the original expression does too, and hence (s−ε)3>2(s-\varepsilon)^3 > 2. This identifies the direction of the estimate. In the next subsection, we will discuss how to construct such an upper bound and use it to choose ε\varepsilon.

3.2. Auxiliary Constraints

Returning to the inequality

3s2ε−3sε2+ε3<s3−2, 3s^2\varepsilon-3s\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^3 \lt s^3-2,

the main difficulty is the presence of higher powers of ε\varepsilon. We would like to replace them with expressions that are linear in ε\varepsilon, so that choosing ε\varepsilon becomes straightforward.

A standard idea is to impose the additional constraint

0<ε<s. 0 \lt \varepsilon \lt s.

Why are we allowed to do this? Here s>0s > 0 is fixed, and we are free to choose ε\varepsilon: we only need one positive value that works. Restricting our search to (0,s)(0,s) is therefore legitimate, provided that we eventually find a value in this interval satisfying the original inequality. We are imposing a sufficient condition, not claiming that every possible solution must satisfy this restriction.

Under this constraint, we can replace selected factors of ε\varepsilon by the larger quantity ss. For example,

ε2≤sε,ε3≤s2ε. \varepsilon^2 \leq s\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon^3 \leq s^2\varepsilon.

The direction of the estimate still matters. Multiplying an inequality by a negative coefficient reverses its direction, so replacing ε2\varepsilon^2 by sεs\varepsilon in the term −3sε2-3s\varepsilon^2 would make that term smaller. That would not give the upper bound we need.

For our present expression, it is more useful to group the last two terms. Since ε<s<3s\varepsilon \lt s \lt 3s,

3s2ε−3sε2+ε3=3s2ε+ε2(ε−3s)≤3s2ε.\begin{aligned} 3s^2\varepsilon-3s\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^3 &= 3s^2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2(\varepsilon-3s) \\ &\leq 3s^2\varepsilon. \end{aligned}

Thus it is enough to require 3s2ε<s3−23s^2\varepsilon \lt s^3-2, together with 0<ε<s0\lt \varepsilon\lt s. The choice used earlier,

ε1=min⁡{s2,s3−26s2}, \varepsilon_1 = \min\left\{\frac{s}{2},\frac{s^3-2}{6s^2}\right\},

satisfies both requirements: it is positive, is at most s/2s/2, and gives 3s2ε1≤(s3−2)/2<s3−23s^2\varepsilon_1 \leq (s^3-2)/2 \lt s^3-2.

The same constraint also explains the estimate in the other case, s3<2s^3\lt 2. There all the error terms are positive, so replacing some factors of ε\varepsilon by ss gives

3s2ε+3sε2+ε3≤3s2ε+3s2ε+s2ε=7s2ε.\begin{aligned} 3s^2\varepsilon+3s\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^3 &\leq 3s^2\varepsilon+3s^2\varepsilon+s^2\varepsilon \\ &= 7s^2\varepsilon. \end{aligned}

It is therefore enough to choose 0<ε<s0\lt \varepsilon\lt s with 7s2ε<2−s37s^2\varepsilon\lt 2-s^3. This leads to the earlier choice

ε2=min⁡{s2,2−s314s2}. \varepsilon_2 = \min\left\{\frac{s}{2},\frac{2-s^3}{14s^2}\right\}.

Why not replace every occurrence of ε\varepsilon by ss? Even when all coefficients are positive and the direction is valid, this can make the estimate too coarse. For instance, the last error expression would be bounded by 7s37s^3, a fixed quantity that does not become smaller as we decrease ε\varepsilon. The resulting sufficient condition 7s3<2−s37s^3\lt 2-s^3 need not hold; indeed, it fails when s≥1s\geq1, as in our example. This would leave us with an unusable estimate, even though suitable small values of ε\varepsilon exist.

The useful principle is to keep one factor of ε\varepsilon and bound the remaining factors. This turns higher-order terms into a constant multiple of ε\varepsilon, preserving our ability to make the error as small as needed.

Once we have listed all the constraints, how do we choose a value satisfying them simultaneously? For finitely many real bounds a1,…,ana_1,\ldots,a_n and b1,…,bnb_1,\ldots,b_n, where nn is a positive integer, maxima and minima provide explicit choices.

Mathematical environments

Definition 1 — Upper bound

Let A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R}. A number M∈RM \in \mathbb{R} is an upper bound of AA if x≤Mx \leq M for every x∈Ax \in A.

Axiom 2 — Completeness

Every nonempty subset of R\mathbb{R} that is bounded above has a supremum in R\mathbb{R}.

Lemma 3 — Approximation from below

If s=sup⁡As = \sup A, then for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0 there exists a∈Aa \in A such that

s−ε<a≤s. s - \varepsilon < a \leq s.

Theorem 4 — Uniqueness of the supremum

A nonempty subset of R\mathbb{R} has at most one supremum.

Proof.

Suppose ss and tt are both suprema of AA. Since tt is an upper bound and ss is the least upper bound, s≤ts \leq t. Similarly, t≤st \leq s. Therefore s=ts = t.

□
Corollary 5

If AA has a maximum mm, then sup⁡A=m\sup A = m.

Example 6 — A supremum without a maximum

Let A=(0,1)A = (0,1). Then sup⁡A=1\sup A = 1, but AA has no maximum because 1∉A1 \notin A.

For every x∈Ax \in A, the number (x+1)/2(x+1)/2 also belongs to AA and is strictly greater than xx.

Remark 7 — Supremum versus maximum

The supremum need not belong to the set. For instance, sup⁡(0,1)=1\sup(0,1)=1, although 1∉(0,1)1 \notin (0,1). This distinction is why an upper bound and a maximum are different notions.
